clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic HOGA1 mutations affecting mitochondrial 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate aldolase in the hydroxyproline degradation pathway.
Frequently the earliest of the three types to present, often with recurrent calcium oxalate stones in infancy or early childhood.
Despite early stones, it usually carries the best long-term renal prognosis, with progression to end-stage renal failure being uncommon.
Biochemical signature is raised urinary oxalate together with elevated 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate and 2,4-dihydroxyglutarate, the discriminating metabolites.
Hypercalciuria is commonly seen alongside the hyperoxaluria and can confuse the clinical picture.
The precise mechanism linking HOGA1 loss to oxalate overproduction is incompletely understood, involving accumulation of hydroxy-oxoglutarate and its diversion to glyoxylate.
Management is largely conservative with hyperhydration and crystallisation inhibitors, and transplantation is rarely required.
Stone activity may lessen with age in some patients.
reference.pathophysiology: Primary hyperoxaluria type 3 is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting from deficiency of 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate aldolase (HOGA1), a mitochondrial enzyme of the hydroxyproline degradation pathway encoded by HOGA1. Loss of enzyme activity leads to accumulation of 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate and dihydroxyglutarate; the precise route to oxalate overproduction remains debated, but the accumulating intermediates are thought to be cleaved to glyoxylate outside the normal compartment or to inhibit glyoxylate-handling enzymes, so that glyoxylate is diverted to oxalate. The excess oxalate causes urinary calcium oxalate supersaturation with recurrent stones, frequently accompanied by hypercalciuria. Compared with types 1 and 2, oxalate overproduction is generally less relentless and renal parenchymal damage less severe, so nephrocalcinosis, chronic kidney disease and systemic oxalosis are distinctly uncommon, and many patients maintain preserved renal function into adult life.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic hypercalciuric calcium oxalate stone disease
Other paediatric monogenic stone or nephrocalcinosis disorders
additionalInvestigations: Urinary oxalate with 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate and dihydroxyglutarate measurement
Urinary calcium and citrate, as hypercalciuria frequently coexists
Renal tract imaging for stones and, rarely, nephrocalcinosis
redFlags: Unexpectedly rapid decline in renal function, which should prompt review of the diagnosis
Development of nephrocalcinosis, which is atypical and warrants reassessment
Recurrent obstructing stones causing acute kidney injury
Rising plasma oxalate, which is rare in type 3 and should raise concern
reference.prognosis: Type 3 typically has the most benign renal prognosis of the primary hyperoxalurias; despite early and recurrent stone formation, progression to end-stage renal failure is uncommon and most patients retain good renal function. Lifelong monitoring remains prudent because a minority develop chronic kidney disease.
pitfalls: Assuming any hyperoxaluria implies the severe type 1 course and over-treating
Overlooking coexisting hypercalciuria that also needs addressing
Missing the diagnosis when only oxalate is measured without the specific hydroxy-oxoglutarate metabolites
Failing to reconsider the diagnosis if renal function declines unexpectedly
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts
Paediatric and adult nephrology reference texts
management: Sustained maintenance hyperhydration to keep the urine dilute and reduce calcium oxalate supersaturation
Potassium citrate and other crystallisation inhibitors to counter stone formation and any hypocitraturia
Management of the frequently coexisting hypercalciuria with dietary sodium restriction and, where marked, a thiazide diuretic, while maintaining adequate dietary calcium
Active but nephron-sparing stone clearance by lithotripsy or endourology for recurrent calculi
Longitudinal monitoring of renal function, urinary oxalate and the discriminating metabolites, and of stone activity
Reassurance regarding the generally favourable renal prognosis, with continued surveillance since a minority develop chronic kidney disease
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive HOGA1 inheritance
